Alistair’s face, when he emerged from the library an hour later, was one of pure relief; the storm had passed, and the sun shone once more upon his romantic ambitions. He clapped me on the shoulder with a heartiness that was in itself a proclamation of victory.

“Well, Finch, what do you say to that?” he cried, his voice booming through the hall. “A complete misunderstanding, the whole of it! Blackwood is a capital fellow, really. A bit eccentric, perhaps, but his heart is in the right place.”

“He explained himself, then?” I asked, following him into the drawing room, where he poured two generous glasses of whisky.

“Explained himself and then some,” Alistair said, handing me a glass. “It seems he has a tragic story. He had a sister, years ago, who was taken in by some handsome scoundrel. A man with a title and no fortune, who wooed her, won her, and then abandoned her when her dowry was spent. The poor girl was ruined, utterly heartbroken. Blackwood has never forgiven himself for not seeing through the fellow sooner. He says he saw me, a man of some means and position, paying attentions to his ward, and his old fears got the better of him. He thought I was just another predator.”

“And you believe this story?” I could not help the note of scepticism from entering my voice. The transformation from raging demon to contrite guardian seemed altogether too swift, too convenient.

“Of course I believe it! Why should I not?” Alistair retorted, though without any real heat. “It explains everything; his possessiveness, his violent temper, the way he has kept her so secluded. He sees a threat in every shadow. He confessed he has been watching me since I arrived, making enquiries, and until today, he was not convinced of my character. Our little scene at the cove was the final straw for him, the proof that I was dishonourable.”

“And what changed his mind in the space of a few hours?”

“My own sincerity, old man,” Alistair declared, puffing out his chest a little. “When I stood up to him, when I told him in no uncertain terms that my intentions were to make Miss Vance my wife, it was the very thing he needed to hear. The other fellow, the scoundrel, had only ever spoken of love in whispers and stolen glances. I, on the other hand, was ready to declare myself before the world. He says he misjudged me completely, and that he is a crusty, overprotective old fool. He begged my pardon a dozen times over.”

It was plausible enough, I had to admit. Men are often shaped by the sorrows of their past, and such a trauma could indeed breed a fierce and irrational protectiveness. And yet, a seed of doubt remained within me. I recalled the look on the girl’s face as her guardian had dragged her away; it was not relief, nor simple obedience. It was terror.

“So what are the terms?” I asked. “Are you now free to see her as you wish?”

“Well, there are some conditions, naturally,” Alistair said, a little of his jubilation fading. “He has asked that we proceed slowly. He wants me to win his trust as well as her affection. We may see each other, but only with propriety. No more secret meetings. He has invited the three of us to take a walk along the cliffs tomorrow afternoon, so that we may all become better acquainted. A bit formal, I suppose, but a step in the right direction, wouldn’t you say?”

“A significant step,” I agreed, forcing a smile. For my friend’s sake, I hoped that I was a fool and that his own generous interpretation of the man was the correct one.

The following afternoon was bright and clear, with a pleasant breeze coming in off the sea. We met them not far from the path leading down to the cove. Mr. Blackwood was a picture of civility, dressed in a smart tweed jacket and offering a hand to me as if we were old friends. He was a tall, spare man with a scholar’s stoop, and his light eyes, which Alistair had described as blazing with fury, were today as placid and untroubled as a summer sky.

Miss Vance was as lovely as I had remembered, though she seemed pale and withdrawn. She gave Alistair a shy, fleeting smile, but her eyes kept darting towards her guardian, as if seeking his approval for every breath she took.

Our walk proceeded pleasantly enough on the surface. Alistair was in high spirits, pointing out seabirds and telling amusing anecdotes of his travels. Blackwood proved to be a surprisingly knowledgeable conversationalist, speaking at length on the local geology and the classification of ferns. He seemed to take a particular interest in my own profession, asking several intelligent questions about advances in forensic science. It was all very normal, very civilised, and yet I could not shake a feeling of profound unease. I felt as though we were all actors in a play, and that just beneath the polite dialogue, a darker drama was being enacted.

I took it upon myself to walk with Miss Vance for a time, allowing Alistair and Blackwood to stride on ahead. I spoke to her of neutral subjects: the weather, the beauty of the coastline, a new novel I had been reading. She answered me in quiet monosyllables, her gaze fixed on the ground before her. She was like a beautiful automaton, going through the motions of a conversation without any spark of life or interest.

Then, as we rounded a sharp bend in the cliff path, a gust of wind caught her shawl and sent it fluttering towards the edge. I moved quickly to retrieve it, and as I turned to hand it back to her, our eyes met for a single, unguarded instant. In that instant, I saw it again: the same desperate, hunted look I had witnessed at the cove. Her lips parted as if to speak, but at that moment, Blackwood’s voice called out from further up the path.

“Elara, my dear, do not dawdle! You will catch a chill.”

The mask fell back into place at once. She took the shawl from me with a murmured word of thanks, her fingers cold and trembling against my own. As she did so, however, I felt something small and hard pressed into my palm. It was a swift, almost imperceptible movement, and a second later her hand was gone. I closed my own hand into a fist, my heart beginning to beat a little faster.

The rest of the walk passed in a blur. My mind was entirely occupied with the object in my pocket and the terrifying implications of the girl’s secret gesture. When we parted company at their gate, I made my excuses and hurried back towards our lodgings, leaving a jubilant Alistair to contemplate his successful afternoon.

Once in the privacy of my own room, I opened my hand. There, in the centre of my palm, lay a small, tightly folded piece of paper. It was not a note, as I had half expected, but a page torn from a book, and the paper was brittle and yellowed with age. There was writing on it, a single line in a spidery, brown ink: “Specimen 7, Argiope bruennichi, female. Captured with mate.” Below the writing was a small, exquisitely detailed drawing of a spider, its body striped in brilliant yellow and black.

I stared at the strange message, utterly mystified. What could it mean? Was it a warning? A cry for help? The words themselves were nonsensical, the detached observations of a naturalist. I examined the reverse of the paper. It was blank. I held it up to the light, hoping for a hidden watermark or a message in invisible ink, but there was nothing. The spider, striped like a wasp, seemed to mock me with its eight sinister eyes. Argiope bruennichi. I made a mental note of the name.

My first impulse was to show it to Alistair, but I resisted. He was so thoroughly under the spell of his own romantic narrative that he would surely dismiss it as a strange misunderstanding. He would invent a dozen innocent explanations. Perhaps Miss Vance had been carrying it for her guardian and passed it to me by mistake. Perhaps it was a page from a book she was reading, dropped and then given to me for safekeeping. He would not, could not, see the desperation I had seen in her eyes. No, I was on my own in this.

That evening, I excused myself from dinner, pleading a headache, and made my way to the small public library in the village. It was a dusty, neglected little place, but the librarian was a helpful old man who took a professional pride in his small collection.

“Argiope bruennichi?” he said, peering at me over his spectacles. “A striking creature. The wasp spider. Not native to these shores, you know, not traditionally. It has been making its way north with the warmer seasons. A beautiful but ruthless predator. The female is much larger than the male. In fact,” he added, warming to his subject, “she often consumes him after mating. A rather grim form of matrimony, is it not?”

A cold dread trickled down my spine. “Captured with mate.” Suddenly the naturalist’s note seemed far less nonsensical. It was a metaphor, a terrible, brilliant metaphor for her own situation. She was the spider, captured, and her guardian was the mate she was expected to consume, or be consumed by. But which was which? Was she the predator or the prey?

“Do you have any books on arachnology?” I asked, my voice tight.

“Only one, I’m afraid, but it is a good one.” He led me to a dusty shelf and pulled down a heavy, leather-bound volume: ‘A Comprehensive Study of British and European Arachnids,’ by a Dr. Anselm Blackwood.

The name hit me like a physical blow. I took the book with a trembling hand and opened it to the title page. There it was, in stark black and white. And below the author’s name was a publisher’s note: “Published in London, 1888.”

I spent the next two hours poring over that book, my sense of horror growing with every page I turned. It was a work of genius, there was no doubt of it. The illustrations were masterful, the prose lucid and insightful. But there was a coldness to it, a clinical detachment in the descriptions of predation and death that I found deeply unsettling. The author was clearly a man obsessed.

I searched for any reference to a sister, a family, a personal tragedy. There was nothing. The dedication was simple: “To E.” Just a single initial. Elara?

I returned to our rooms long after midnight, my mind a whirl of suspicion and fear. The story of the ruined sister was a lie. I was sure of it. Blackwood was not a gentleman of leisure; he was a reclusive scholar, an expert on spiders. He had fabricated a persona, a plausible history, to lull Alistair’s suspicions. But why? What was his game?

The next day brought an opportunity. Alistair received a telegram from his solicitors requiring his presence in London for a day or two. He was reluctant to leave, but the business was urgent.

“Look after things here, will you, Finch?” he said, as he boarded the morning train. “And do try to like Blackwood. He’s not so bad once you get to know him.”

I assured him I would, my conscience pricking me for the deception. The moment his train was out of sight, I set my own plan into motion. I had to get into Blackwood’s house. I had to speak to the girl alone.

I made my way towards their isolated villa, my mind racing. A direct approach was out of the question. Blackwood would never allow me a private word with her. I needed a pretext, a way to get past the guardian. My eyes fell upon the medical bag I still carried with me from habit. An idea began to form, a risky and unprofessional plan, but the only one I could devise.

I approached the house from the rear, circling through a patch of overgrown woods that bordered the property. The back of the house was dominated by a large conservatory, its glass panes grimy with dirt. Peering through the foliage, I could see inside. It was not filled with flowers and ferns, as one might expect. It was a nightmare world of glass tanks and terrariums. And inside every tank was a spider. Spiders of every shape and size, some motionless, some weaving intricate webs. It was Blackwood’s laboratory.

A movement at the far end of the conservatory caught my eye. It was Miss Vance, dusting the frame of a large terrarium. She moved with a slow, listless grace, a prisoner tending her own jail. Blackwood was nowhere in sight. This was my chance.

I emerged from the woods and walked briskly to the back door of the house. I did not knock, but tried the handle. It was unlocked. My heart hammered against my ribs as I stepped inside, into a small, dark scullery. I could hear the clatter of pots from a nearby kitchen. A servant. I held my breath, but the sounds continued uninterrupted.

Quietly, I made my way through a dark corridor towards the front of the house, where I knew the library was located. The house was unnervingly silent, filled with a musty smell of old paper and chemicals. I found the library and slipped inside, closing the door softly behind me.

And there he was.

Mr. Blackwood was seated at a large desk, his back to me, so engrossed in the specimen under his microscope that he had not heard me enter. A large diagram of a spider’s nervous system was pinned to the wall above his head. For a moment I simply stood there, watching him, my resolve hardening.

“Mr. Blackwood,” I said, my voice louder than I intended.

He sprang from his chair, spinning around with a speed that was astonishing in a man of his scholarly bearing. The placid mask was gone. His eyes were the ones Alistair had described: pale, cold, and blazing with a sudden, venomous fury.

“What is the meaning of this?” he hissed. “How did you get in here?”

“I have come on a matter of professional urgency,” I said, trying to keep my voice steady. I held up my medical bag. “I received a message that Miss Vance had been taken ill. A sudden fainting spell.”

His eyes narrowed with suspicion. “I have heard of no such thing. Who sent this message?”

“It was delivered to my rooms anonymously. A boy from the village. I came at once, of course.”

For a long moment, he simply stared at me, his sharp mind clearly dissecting my story, searching for its flaws. I met his gaze without flinching, praying my bluff would hold.

“Elara is in perfect health,” he said at last, his voice flat. “You have been the victim of a prank. Now I must ask you to leave.”

“Of course,” I said, turning as if to go. “But since I am here, perhaps I might just look in on her, to set my own mind at ease. As a medical man, you understand.”

“That will not be necessary,” he snapped. “She is not to be disturbed. Good day to you, Mr. Finch.”

His dismissal was absolute. My plan had failed. Dejected, I walked towards the door. But as my hand touched the knob, a new thought, a desperate gamble, came to me.

“A fascinating specimen,” I said, gesturing towards the diagram on the wall. “Is that a Tegenaria, a common house spider?”

He was momentarily taken aback by the change of subject. “It is,” he said grudgingly.

“My interests run to the more exotic, I confess,” I went on, my voice casual. “A colleague of mine in London recently acquired a magnificent female Argiope bruennichi. The wasp spider. A truly formidable creature.”

The effect of my words was instantaneous and terrifying. Every trace of colour drained from Blackwood’s face. His hands, which were resting on the desk, clenched into white-knuckled fists. He looked at me, and in his eyes, I saw not just anger, but the raw panic of a man whose deepest secret has been exposed.

“What do you know of that?” he whispered, his voice a dry rasp.

“Only what I read,” I said softly. “And that the female has a rather brutal way of dealing with her mates.”

Before he could answer, the library door opened, and Miss Vance stood on the threshold.

“I heard voices,” she said, her eyes wide with alarm as she took in the scene. She looked from my face to her guardian’s, and her hand flew to her mouth.

“It is all right, Elara,” Blackwood said, his voice regaining some of its composure, though his face was still a ghastly white. “Mr. Finch was just leaving.”

But I was not leaving. I moved to stand beside the girl, placing myself between her and the man at the desk.

“Miss Vance,” I said, speaking to her directly. “My friend, Alistair, has been called to London. But he asked me to watch over you. He is a good man, an honourable man, and he loves you. If you are in any danger, you must tell me now.”

She stared at me, her eyes filled with a desperate, agonizing indecision. She looked at Blackwood, who stood rigid, like a serpent about to strike.

“Tell him to go, Elara,” Blackwood commanded, his voice low and menacing. “Tell him he is mistaken.”

The girl trembled, and for a moment I thought she would obey. But then she took a deep breath, and a flicker of defiance, of the courage I had so longed to see, ignited in her eyes.

“No,” she whispered, her voice barely audible. Then, louder, she repeated it. “No. He is not mistaken. He is my husband.”

The confession hung in the air, monstrous and final. My own theories had not stretched so far as this.

“Husband?” I echoed, stunned.

“He married me two years ago,” she said, her words coming in a rush now that the dam of her silence had broken. “My father was his mentor, a fellow academic. When he died, he left me in Anselm’s care. He controls my inheritance. He brought me here to this wretched place and told the world I was his ward. He has kept me a prisoner.”

“Silence, you ungrateful wretch!” Blackwood snarled, taking a step forward.

His sister’s terror, her desperate warnings for Sir Henry to leave, all became terrifyingly clear. He strode towards the main house, and I heard his voice call out in a sharp, peremptory tone.

I knew from my studies of the ordnance maps with Holmes that most of the streams on this part of the moor eventually fed into the lower lands near the villages. It was a slim hope, but it was all I had.

The night was endless. Every shadow seemed to hold a new threat, every rustle of the wind in the reeds sounded like the footstep of my pursuer. My mind, overwrought with exhaustion and fear, began to play tricks on me. I saw the glint of Stapleton’s spectacles in every moonbeam that broke through the clouds, heard his thin, cruel voice in the cry of a nocturnal bird. I thought of Sir Henry, sitting peacefully at dinner, perhaps raising a glass with the very man whose accomplice was now being consumed by the bog, and the thought gave me a renewed, if frantic, strength. I had to warn him. I had to get back.

The first grey hint of dawn was staining the eastern sky when I finally saw it: a familiar landmark. It was the dark, jagged shape of the quarry on the hill from which I had watched Sir Henry and Miss Stapleton that fateful afternoon. I knew my way from there. With a sob of relief, I staggered towards it, my body a mass of aches and bruises, my clothes torn and caked in mud. I was a scarecrow of a man, but I was alive, and I was free.

From the crest of the hill, I could see the chimneys of Merripit House, a thin plume of smoke already rising from one of them. The sight spurred me on. I half ran, half fell down the slope, my mind now focused on a new problem: how to get inside without alerting the murderer who might well be at the breakfast table.

I did not go to the front door. Instead, I crept around to the back, to the kitchens, hoping to find a sympathetic servant. As luck would have it, the scullery window had been left unlatched. It was a tight squeeze, but I managed to hoist my aching body through, tumbling in a heap onto the cold stone floor, much to the astonishment of a young maid who was just beginning her morning’s work.

She gave a small scream, which I quickly stifled with a hand and a desperate plea. “Not a word,” I whispered, my voice a hoarse croak. “Where is Sir Henry?”

The girl, her eyes wide with fright at my wild appearance, pointed a trembling finger towards the front of the house. “In the dining room, sir. With Mr. Stapleton. He came back late last night, said he was worried for you, and stayed the night.”

My blood ran cold. Stapleton was here. He had beaten me back. He was with Sir Henry now, playing the part of the concerned friend, while I had been fighting for my life on the moor. He must have given up his search and returned, concocting some story to explain his presence and my absence.

There was no time for subtlety. I burst from the kitchens and ran down the hall, ignoring the maid’s frightened gasp. I threw open the dining room door with such force that it crashed against the wall.

The scene before me was one of perfect domestic peace. Sir Henry and Stapleton were seated at the table, a hearty breakfast spread between them. Sir Henry was just lifting a coffee cup to his lips. He looked up, his eyes widening in utter astonishment at my appearance.

“Good God, Watson!” he exclaimed, dropping his cup with a clatter. “Man, what in heaven’s name has happened to you? We have been worried half to death!”

Stapleton, however, showed no such surprise. He had risen slowly to his feet, his face pale, but his eyes were blazing with a cold, reptilian fury. The mask was gone. In his gaze I saw not the mild-mannered naturalist, but the cornered killer. He had lost his henchman, lost his prisoner, and now his deception was at an end.

“So,” he said, his voice soft and deadly. “The good doctor returns from his little nocturnal ramble. I must confess, I did not expect to see you again.”

“Stapleton,” I gasped, pointing a trembling, mud-caked finger at him. “Sir Henry, this man is a murderer! He tried to kill me! He is not Stapleton, he is a Baskerville! He is the one who has been terrorizing you!”

Sir Henry looked from my frantic face to Stapleton’s cold one, his expression a mixture of confusion and dawning horror. “Watson, you’re not making any sense. A Baskerville? What are you talking about?”

“His wife,” I croaked, my throat raw. “The woman you know as his sister, she is his wife! He brought her here to lure you, to use her as bait! He killed your uncle, Sir Charles, with a giant hound, and he intended to do the same to you! Last night, he took me to the Grimpen Mire to murder me!”

Stapleton let out a short, sharp laugh, a sound devoid of all mirth. “My dear Sir Henry, you must excuse the doctor. The moor can be a disorienting place. It seems the poor fellow has had a fall and addled his wits. I found his hat near the mire last night and feared the worst. I have been searching for him all night. It seems he has had some sort of fever-dream.”

He was good. He was terribly good. His calm denial, my own wild appearance; I could see the doubt warring with concern in Sir Henry’s eyes.

“It is no dream!” I insisted, taking a step into the room. “He has an accomplice, a brute named Murphy! He is at the bottom of the bog, Stapleton, and that is where you belong!”

At the mention of Murphy, a flicker of something, a momentary loss of composure, crossed Stapleton’s face. He knew I was speaking the truth. Sir Henry saw it too.

“Stapleton,” the baronet said, his voice low and dangerous as he rose from his chair. “What is the meaning of this?”

Stapleton knew the game was up. His hand darted inside his jacket. But I was ready for him. All the fear and fury of the past twelve hours culminated in a single, primal instinct. With a cry, I launched myself across the breakfast table, scattering plates and silverware. I crashed into him, and we went down together in a heap, my hands scrabbling for his, trying to stop him from drawing the pistol I knew he must be carrying.

Sir Henry, his face a grim mask of understanding and betrayal, was on us in an instant. The baronet, for all his fine manners, was a strong man, hardened by a life in the colonies. He seized Stapleton’s arms from behind, pinning him to the floor.

“It’s true, then,” Sir Henry said, his voice choked with rage and disillusionment. “Everything Watson said. It’s all true.”

Stapleton ceased his struggling. He lay on the floor beneath us, his chest heaving, but a strange, triumphant smile played on his thin lips.

“You have won this little skirmish, Doctor,” he wheezed, his cold eyes fixed on me. “But the game is not over. You have forgotten about the hound.”

A chill, colder than any I had felt on the moor, ran down my spine. We had him, but his final threat still hung in the air. We were two men in a locked room with a killer, and his most terrible weapon was, we knew not where, still waiting. The mists of the moor might yet have the final word. I looked at Sir Henry, and in his eyes I saw the same grim realisation. Our ordeal was very far from over.
